notice: Suggested CEFR levels are learning-guide tags, not CEFR certification. These entries have no quiz keys or scoring evidence.

entries.meaning: move to another place
entries.example: Yesterday we went to the sports centre after lunch.
entries.note: go — went — gone; use went for the simple past; gone commonly follows have/has.

entries.meaning: notice something with your eyes
entries.example: I saw a colourful bird outside my window.
entries.note: see — saw — seen; avoid 'have saw' in standard English.

entries.meaning: get something by paying for it
entries.example: Nina bought a second-hand dictionary last week.
entries.note: buy — bought — bought; the past and past participle are the same.

entries.meaning: make words on paper or a screen
entries.example: We have written three short reviews this month.
entries.note: write — wrote — written; use the participle after have/has.

entries.meaning: decide between possibilities
entries.example: The class chose a new team name on Monday.
entries.note: choose — chose — chosen; don't confuse present choose with past chose.

entries.meaning: become larger or develop
entries.example: The plants have grown quickly in the sunny room.
entries.note: grow — grew — grown; grown often follows have/has.

entries.meaning: get onto a bus you planned to travel on
entries.example: If we leave now, we can catch the early bus.
entries.note: We usually say catch a bus, not take hold of a bus.

entries.meaning: write short points while listening or reading
entries.example: I take notes during science videos to remember key ideas.
entries.note: Take notes is a common verb–noun combination.

entries.meaning: improve or move towards a goal
entries.example: Her reading is difficult, but she is making progress.
entries.note: We say make progress; progress is normally uncountable here.

entries.meaning: finish work by the required time
entries.example: The team divided the tasks so they could meet the deadline.
entries.note: Meet a deadline means finish on time, not meet a person.

entries.meaning: reasoning supported by good reasons or evidence
entries.example: Their proposal gives a strong argument for a quieter library.
entries.note: Strong describes the quality of reasoning, not speaking loudly.

entries.meaning: search for information in a reference source
entries.example: You can look up a new word in a dictionary.
entries.note: Separable: look the word up is possible; look up the word is also possible.

entries.meaning: have no more of something left
entries.example: We ran out of paper before the art lesson finished.
entries.note: Run out of something does not mean run outdoors.

entries.meaning: reject an offer or request
entries.example: Kai turned down the invitation because he had another plan.
entries.note: Turn down is also used for lowering volume; context changes its meaning.

entries.meaning: organize or prepare something so it can start
entries.example: Students set up a small exhibition in the hallway.
entries.note: Set up can be separable: set the display up.

entries.meaning: help people feel more relaxed when first meeting
entries.example: A simple question about music helped break the ice at the club.
entries.note: This is figurative: no real ice needs to break.

entries.meaning: feeling slightly ill
entries.example: I felt under the weather, so I rested after school.
entries.note: A conversational idiom, not a medical diagnosis.

entries.meaning: agree on the basic understanding or plan
entries.example: Before starting, the group checked they were on the same page.
entries.note: Common in teamwork; it is not about reading one literal page.

entries.meaning: many with countable plural nouns; much with uncountable nouns
entries.example: How many pencils do you need? How much water is left?
entries.note: Ask whether the noun can be counted as individual items.

entries.meaning: since names a starting point; for gives a duration
entries.example: I have lived here since 2022. I have lived here for four years.
entries.note: Since and for express different kinds of time information.

entries.meaning: borrow means receive temporarily; lend means give temporarily
entries.example: Can I borrow your ruler? Yes, I can lend it to you.
entries.note: Check who receives the object and who gives it.

entries.meaning: fewer usually modifies countable plurals; less usually modifies uncountable nouns
entries.example: This version has fewer errors and needs less time.
entries.note: These are useful general writing conventions; some real-world usage varies.

entries.meaning: first identify what the whole passage is about
entries.example: Before checking dates, read the headline and ask what the notice is for.
entries.note: A gist answer should describe the main message, not repeat one small fact.

entries.meaning: separate what a text supports from what you only suppose
entries.example: If a poster says places are limited, do not assume every applicant is accepted.
entries.note: Point to an actual sentence before making a strong inference.

entries.meaning: decide what a sentence needs to express before choosing a grammar pattern
entries.example: If an action ended yesterday, check whether a simple past form is appropriate.
entries.note: Compare meanings first; then check forms and common exceptions.

entries.meaning: identify Topic, Task, Must Include and Boundary before drafting
entries.example: For a school invitation, note who will read it and which details they need.
entries.note: Brainstorm useful ideas, outline briefly, then check whether the final text answers the task.
